parts.latex:
Kenzo is driving his car along a road while his friend records the velocity of the car, $v(t)$, in km/h every minute over a 5-minute period. The table gives the velocity $v(t)$ at time $t$ hours.

\extable{Tp331_1}

The distance covered by the car over the 5-minute period is given by

$$\int_0^{\frac{5}{60}} v(t)\,dt.$$

Use the trapezoidal rule and the velocity at each of the six time values to find the approximate distance in kilometres the car has travelled in the 5-minute period. Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\frac{5}{60} - 0}{2(5)}\Big[60 + 67 + 2(55 + 65 + 68 + 70)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{643}{120} \\ &\approx 5.4 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the trapezoidal rule

231.stem:
The diagram shows two parabolas $y=4x-x^2$ and $y=ax^2$, where $a>0$. The two parabolas intersect at the origin, $O$, and at $A$.

\exfigure{34_q30_1}

figures.cap: parabolas y=4x-x^2 and y=ax^2 with shaded region between O and A

parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{4}{a+1}$.
Find the value of $a$ such that the shaded area is $\dfrac{16}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} ax^2 &= 4x - x^2 \\ (a+1)x^2 - 4x &= 0 \\ x\left[(a+1)x - 4\right] &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$x = 0 \text{ or } (a+1)x - 4 = 0$$
$$\begin{aligned} (a+1)x &= 4 \\ x &= \dfrac{4}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{4}{a+1}$.
criteria: Attempts to solve a quadratic equation to find the $x$-coordinate of $A$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{4}{a+1}} \left(4x - x^2 - ax^2\right)dx &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \int_0^{\frac{4}{a+1}} \left(4x - (a+1)x^2\right)dx &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \left[2x^2 - \dfrac{(a+1)x^3}{3}\right]_0^{\frac{4}{a+1}} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{2\times 16}{(a+1)^2} - \dfrac{(a+1)}{3}\times\dfrac{64}{(a+1)^3} - 0 &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{32}{(a+1)^2} - \dfrac{64}{3(a+1)^2} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{96 - 64}{3(a+1)^2} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{32}{3(a+1)^2} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ (a+1)^2 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = \sqrt{2} - 1 \qquad (\text{since } a > 0)$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes the limits into the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit
Finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit
Writes an expression for the area involving an integral of the difference between two functions, or equivalent merit

circle x^2+y^2=2 and hyperbola y=a/(b-x)-1 through O and (1,1); region bounded by hyperbola, positive x-axis and circle shaded

parts.latex: By considering the value of $\theta$, find the exact area of the shaded region, as shown on the diagram.
Using parts (a) and (b), find the exact area of the region bounded by the hyperbola, the positive $x$-axis and the circle as shown on the diagram.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x = y = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{a}{b} - 1 \\ \therefore\ \dfrac{a}{b} &= 1 \\ \therefore\ a &= b \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x = y = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \dfrac{a}{b - 1} - 1 \\ 1 &= \dfrac{a}{a - 1} - 1 \\ \dfrac{a}{a - 1} &= 2 \\ a &= 2a - 2 \\ \therefore\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b = 2$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area under curve (hyperbola)} &= \int_0^1 \left(\dfrac{2}{2 - x} - 1\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-2\ln(2 - x) - x\Big]_0^1 \\ &= -2\ln 1 - 1 + 2\ln 2 - 0 \\ &= 2\ln 2 - 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area} &= 2\ln 2 - 1 + \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 2\ln 2 + \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{3}{2} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Gives the area as a sum of an integral and the area from part (a), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The diagram shows the graph $y=f(x)$, where $f(x)$ is an odd function.

The shaded area is 1 square unit.

The number $a$, where $a>1$, is chosen so that $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=0$.

\exfigure{296_q5_1}

What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
The shaded region between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ is below the $x$-axis with area $1$:
$$\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = -1$$
$f$ is odd, so $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0$, and
$$\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx + \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$$
By odd symmetry, $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx = -\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = 0$.
$$\therefore\ \int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx = 0 + (-1) = -1$$

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is an odd function.
Hence, or otherwise, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-\pi$ to $x=\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Show that $-f(x)=f(-x)$.

$$-f(x)=-2x+\sin x$$

$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=2(-x)-\sin(-x)\\ &=-2x-(-\sin x)\\ &=-2x+\sin x\\ &=-f(x)\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore\ f(x)$ is an odd function.

Using the symmetry property of $f(x)$ from part (a):

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_0^{\pi}(2x-\sin x)\,dx\\ &=2\Big[x^2+\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi}\\ &=2\big((\pi^2+\cos\pi)-(0^2+\cos 0)\big)\\ &=2(\pi^2-2)\\ &=2\pi^2-4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Determines the definite integral without considering the signed area, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: curve y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4 with trapezia, heights 4, 5.125, 13

solutions.latex:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$

Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$

$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$

$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.
criteria: Finds the area using integration and the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using either the trapezoidal rule or integration, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graphs of y=x^3-2x and y=x^2 with shaded regions

parts.latex:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=x^3-2x$ and $y=x^2$.

\exfigure{510_q33_1}

The graphs intersect at $A$, $B$ and the origin, $O$.

By finding the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, show that the area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{37}{12}$.

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-2x &= x^2 \\ x^3-x^2-2x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-x-2) &= 0 \\ x(x+1)(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $2$.

Area between the two curves is given by
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly sets up a sum of two integrals, including correct bounds for each integral, and attempts to find the area between the two curves, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating the functions, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graphs of y=(x-1)^2 and y=2x-2 intersecting at (1,0) and (3,4), shaded regions from x=0 to x=3

parts.latex:
The area of the shaded region in the diagram below is given by:

\exfigure{568_q6_1}

solutions.latex:
From the diagram, the shaded region has two parts.

For $0 \le x \le 1$ the parabola $y = (x-1)^2$ is above the line $y = 2x - 2$, so the area is
$$\int_0^1\big((x-1)^2 - (2x-2)\big)dx = \int_0^1\big((x-1)^2 - 2x + 2\big)dx$$

For $1 \le x \le 3$ the line is above the parabola (they meet at $(1, 0)$ and $(3, 4)$), so the area is
$$\int_1^3\big((2x-2) - (x-1)^2\big)dx$$

Total area:
$$\int_0^1\big((x-1)^2 - 2x + 2\big)dx + \int_1^3\big((2x-2) - (x-1)^2\big)dx$$

parts.latex: Find the area bounded by $y=\ln x$ and the y-axis from $y=0$ to $y=\ln 3$.

solutions.latex:
The region lies between the curve and the $y$-axis, so integrate with respect to $y$.

From $y = \ln x$, $x = e^y$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{\ln 3}e^y\,dy \\ &= \Big[e^y\Big]_0^{\ln 3} \\ &= e^{\ln 3} - e^0 \\ &= 3 - 1 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The area is $2$ square units.

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with 2 subintervals to find in simplest exact form an approximation for $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Two subintervals from $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so the width of each is
$$h=\dfrac{\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{6}}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
and the function values are needed at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $f(x)=\dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}$:

\extable{Ts25_1}

By the trapezoidal rule,
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
with $\dfrac{h}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left\{(2+\sqrt{3})+2\sqrt{3}+1\right\}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}(3+3\sqrt{3})\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{4}(1+\sqrt{3})\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Hence show in simplest exact form that the region enclosed by the two curves has area $2\sqrt{5}$ square units.

$\therefore\ \tan x=2$, $0\le x\le 2\pi$

meta.top_criterion_original: Explains why the $x$ coordinates of intersection points satisfy $\tan x=2$

solutions.latex:
Area is given by
$$A=\int_\alpha^{\pi+\alpha}(\sin x-2\cos x)\,dx$$
where $0<\alpha<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan\alpha=2$.

[Right triangle with opposite 2, adjacent 1, hypotenuse $\sqrt{5}$.]
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left[-\cos x-2\sin x\right]_\alpha^{\pi+\alpha}\\ &=-\{\cos(\pi+\alpha)-\cos\alpha\}-2[\sin(\pi+\alpha)-\sin\alpha]\\ &=2\cos\alpha+4\sin\alpha\\ &=2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}$$
Area enclosed by the two curves is $2\sqrt{5}$ sq. units.

The region is between the curve and the $y$-axis, from $y = 1$ ($x = 0$) to $y = 4$ ($x = 2$).

It is the rectangle $0 \le x \le 2$, $0 \le y \le 4$ minus the area under the curve from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\times 4 - \int_0^2 2^x\,dx \\ &= 8 - \left[\dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2}\right]_0^2 \\ &= 8 - \dfrac{4 - 1}{\ln 2} \\ &= 8 - \dfrac{3}{\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Show that $-f(x)=f(-x)$.
$$-f(x)=-2x+\sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=2(-x)-\sin(-x)\\ &=-2x-(-\sin x)\\ &=-2x+\sin x\\ &=-f(x)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)$ is an odd function.

Using the symmetry property of $f(x)$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_0^{\pi}(2x-\sin x)\,dx\\ &=2\Big[x^2+\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi}\\ &=2\big((\pi^2+\cos\pi)-(0^2+\cos 0)\big)\\ &=2(\pi^2-2)\\ &=2\pi^2-4\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The graph below shows the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4$.

Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$, determine how much the Trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve. \exfigure{1346_q30_1}

solutions.latex:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$
$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$
$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.
criteria: Finds the area using integration and the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using either the trapezoidal rule or integration, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=x^3-2x$ and $y=x^2$. \exfigure{1346_q33_1} The graphs intersect at $A$, $B$ and the origin, $O$.

By finding the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, show that the area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{37}{12}$.

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-2x &= x^2 \\ x^3-x^2-2x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-x-2) &= 0 \\ x(x+1)(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $2$.

Area between the two curves is given by
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly sets up a sum of two integrals, including correct bounds for each integral, and attempts to find the area between the two curves, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A function $f(x)$ is given such that: $$\int_{-k}^{k} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{k} f(x)\,dx.$$ Which of the following could be a possible function for $f(x)$?

solutions.latex:
Splitting the integral at $0$:
$$\int_{-k}^{k} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-k}^{0} f(x)\,dx + \int_{0}^{k} f(x)\,dx$$
So the condition says $\displaystyle\int_{-k}^{0} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{k} f(x)\,dx$: the area on the left of the $y$-axis equals the area on the right. This is true when $f$ is even (its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis).

$\sin 2x$, $\tan 2x$ and $\operatorname{cosec} 2x$ are odd functions; $\cos 2x$ is even, since $\cos(-2x)=\cos 2x$.

$\therefore$ $f(x)=\cos 2x$.

parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x-x\cos x)=x\sin x.$$
Hence, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{2025\pi}x\sin x\,dx$.

The regions bounded by the $x$-axis and the graph of $y=x\sin x$ for $x\ge 0$ are shown.

\exfigure{1630_q25_1}

Let $A_n=\displaystyle\int_{(n-1)\pi}^{n\pi}x\sin x\,dx$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

It can be shown that $\left|A_n\right|=(2n-1)\pi$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find the exact total area of the regions bounded by the curve $y=x\sin x$, and the $x$-axis between $x=0$ and $x=2025\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $x\cos x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x-x\cos x) &= \cos x-\left[x\times(-\sin x)+\cos x\right] \\ &= \cos x+x\sin x-\cos x \\ &= x\sin x \quad\text{as required} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\sin x-x\cos x$ is a primitive of $x\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{2025\pi}x\sin x\,dx &= \Big[\sin x-x\cos x\Big]_0^{2025\pi} \\ &= (\sin 2025\pi-2025\pi\cos 2025\pi)-(0) \\ &= 0-2025\pi\times(-1) \\ &= 2025\pi \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses part (a) to rewrite the definite integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total area is $|A_1|+|A_2|+\cdots+|A_{2025}|$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Exact area of regions} &= \pi+3\pi+5\pi+\cdots+(2\times 2025-1)\pi \\ &= \pi+3\pi+5\pi+\cdots+4049\pi \end{aligned}$$
This is an arithmetic series with $a=\pi$, $d=2\pi$, $n=2025$ and $l=4049\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}(a+l) \\ S_n &= \dfrac{2025}{2}(\pi+4049\pi) \\ &= 2025\times 2025\times\pi \\ &= (2025)^2\pi \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sums an arithmetic sequence, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the shaded region.
Show that the exact area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{3}{4\ln 2}$.
Using your answers from part (a) and part (b), deduce $e<2\sqrt{2}$.

solutions.latex:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule use $n=2$ strips:
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{2}=1$$
so $x_0=0$, $x_1=1$, $x_2=2$, with
$$f(0)=1, \quad f(1)=\dfrac{1}{2}, \quad f(2)=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\Big\{f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)\right]\Big\} \\ &= \dfrac{2-0}{2\times 2}\left\{1+\dfrac{1}{4}+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{4}+1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x dx &= \left[\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^0}{\ln\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-\frac{3}{4}}{-\ln 2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides the correct antiderivative of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The function is concave up, so the exact value is less than the trapezoidal approximation:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} &< \dfrac{9}{8} \\ 24 &< 36\ln 2 \\ 2 &< 3\ln 2 \\ 2 &< \ln 8 \\ e^2 &< 8 \\ e &< \sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ e<2\sqrt{2}$$
criteria: Provides correct initial inequality, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A section of the graph of $y=f(x)$ for $x\ge 0$ is shown, where $f(x)$ is an odd function.

\exfigure{1632_q8_1}

Four integrals based on this graph are given.

$$\begin{array}{r@{\;}l@{\qquad\qquad}r@{\;}l} P= & \displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx & R= & \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx \\[3ex] Q= & \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx & S= & \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx \end{array}$$

Which of the following options identifies the integrals in ascending numerical order?

solutions.latex:
Let $A_1$ be the area between the curve and the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le 1$ (above the axis) and $A_2$ the area for $1\le x\le a$ (below the axis). From the grid, $A_1>2A_2$.

$f$ is odd, so the integral over $[-a,a]$ is $0$ and the integral over $[-a,0]$ is the negative of the integral over $[0,a]$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=A_1-A_2>0\\ Q&=0\\ R&=Q-\int_1^a f(x)\,dx=A_2\\ S&=-P \end{aligned}$$
Since $A_1-A_2>A_2>0$, the order is $S<Q<R<P$.

parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinates of the two points of intersection are $x=-1$ and $x=5$.
Hence find the area enclosed by the line $y=7-3x$ and the parabola $y=-x^2+x+12$.

solutions.latex:
At the points of intersection the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 7-3x&=-x^2+x+12\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-1 \text{ or } x=5$$
criteria: Equates the two functions to form a quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Substituted x=-1 (y=10 both) and x=5 (y=-8 both).

solutions.latex:
Between $x=-1$ and $x=5$ the parabola is above the line (at $x=0$: $12>7$), so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line):
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-1}^{5}\big((-x^2+x+12)-(7-3x)\big)\,dx\\ &=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{125}{3}+50+25\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\ &=\dfrac{100}{3}+\dfrac{8}{3}\\ &=36\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=36 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes a correct integral for the area, or equivalent merit

624.stem:
Let $g(t)$ be a function defined for all $t\ge 0$. The gradient function is given by

$$g'(t)=\dfrac{33}{10}te^{-kt}.$$

where $k$ is a positive constant. The diagram below shows a sketch of $g'(t)$ against $t$.

It is given that $g'(t)$ attains the greatest value at $t=7.5$ and $g(0)=0$.

\exfigure{1369_q30_1}

figures.cap: graph of g'(t) shaded from 0 to 12 with strips at 3, 6, 9

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{15}$.

Stationary points and their nature.evidence: g'(t) has its greatest value at t=7.5, so g''(7.5)=0
Stationary points and their nature.reason: Locating the maximum of g' via its derivative = 0 is the key step.

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with four sub-intervals to estimate the shaded area in the diagram.
Explain why your answer to part (b) is an estimate for $g(12)$.

Rates of change using integration.reason: Integrating a given rate g'(t) to get the quantity g(12).

Trapezoidal rule.evidence: The trapezoidal estimate from part (b) approximates the shaded area

solutions.latex:
$g'(t)$ has its greatest value at $t=7.5$, so $g''(7.5)=0$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=t & v&=e^{-kt}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-ke^{-kt}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}g''(t)&=\dfrac{33}{10}\left(e^{-kt}+t(-k)e^{-kt}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{33}{10}e^{-kt}(1-kt)\end{aligned}$$
When $t=7.5$, $g''(t)=0$:
$$\dfrac{33}{10}e^{-7.5k}(1-7.5k)=0$$
Since $e^{-7.5k}\ne 0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-7.5k&=0\\ 7.5k&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{7.5}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{15}\end{aligned}$$

625.stem:
A new luxury hotel in Byron Bay is being designed to feature a stunning wave-shaped window that stretches across the main lobby wall, inspired by the rolling surf of the nearby beaches. The top edge of this window is modelled mathematically to reflect both a smooth curve and a gentle wave.

The height, $h(x)$, of the top edge of the window above ground level, in metres, is described by the piecewise function:

$$h(x)=\begin{cases}a\left(1-(x-1)^2\right), & 0\le x\le 1\\ 2\cos(x-1)+2, & 1<x\le d\end{cases}$$

where $a$ and $d$ are constants and $x$ is the horizontal distance from the leftmost point of the window (which is at ground level).

\exfigure{1369_q31_1}

figures.cap: graph of h(x) from 0 to d
line AB tangent to h(x) at C

parts.latex: Determine the value of $a$ in the function $h(x)$.
By first showing that the length of the bottom edge of the window $d$ is $(\pi+1)$ metres, determine the area of the window.

solutions.latex:
$h(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$, so the two pieces agree there:
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(1-(1-1)^2\right)&=2\cos(1-1)+2\\ a\times 1&=2\cos 0+2\\ a&=2\times 1+2\\ a&=4\end{aligned}$$

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions on scanned pages (no text layer); marking guideline gives no mark criteria; criteria written to house style

solutions.latex:
The right end of the window is at ground level, so $h(d)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos(d-1)+2&=0\\ 2\cos(d-1)&=-2\\ \cos(d-1)&=-1\\ d-1&=\pi\quad(\text{first solution})\\ d&=\pi+1\end{aligned}$$
The area of the window is the area under each piece of $h(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^1 4\left(1-(x-1)^2\right)dx+\int_1^{\pi+1}\left(2\cos(x-1)+2\right)dx\\ &=4\int_0^1\left(2x-x^2\right)dx+2\int_1^{\pi+1}\left(\cos(x-1)+1\right)dx\\ &=4\left[\dfrac{2x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1+2\Big[\sin(x-1)+x\Big]_1^{\pi+1}\\ &=4\left[\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\right]+2\left[\sin\pi+\pi+1-(\sin 0+1)\right]\\ &=\left(\dfrac{8}{3}+2\pi\right)\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
At the intersections the $y$ values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} x-2&=2-\dfrac{3}{x}\\ x^2-4x+3&=0\\ (x-3)(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le 3$ the curve $y=2-\dfrac{3}{x}$ lies above the line $y=x-2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_1^3\left(2-\dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx-\int_1^3(x-2)\,dx\\ &=\int_1^3\left(\left(2-\dfrac{3}{x}\right)-(x-2)\right)dx\\ &=\int_1^3\left(4-\dfrac{3}{x}-x\right)dx\\ &=\left[4x-3\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^3\\ &=4(3)-3\ln 3-\dfrac{3^2}{2}-\left(4(1)-3\ln 1-\dfrac{1^2}{2}\right)\\ &=4-3\ln 3\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (quotient rule for $f'$):
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \ln\left(1+x^2\right)\\ f'(x) &= \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\\ f''(x) &= \dfrac{2\left(1+x^2\right)-2x(2x)}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}\\ &= \dfrac{2-2x^2}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}\end{aligned}$$
The denominator is always positive, so $f''(x)>0$ when
$$\begin{aligned} 2-2x^2 &> 0\\ x^2 &< 1\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1628_q22_s1}
$$\therefore\ f''(x)>0 \text{ for } -1<x<1$$
So $f(x)$ is concave up for $-1<x<1$.
criteria: Finds the correct second derivative, or equivalent merit

$$h=\dfrac{10-1}{3}=3$$
so $x=1,\ 4,\ 7,\ 10$. By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{3}{2}\left[f(1)+2f(4)+2f(7)+f(10)\right] \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln 1+2\ln 4+2\ln 7+\ln 10\right] \\ &=13.45 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

The shaded area is the rectangle $10\times\ln 10$ minus the region between the curve and the $y$-axis for $0\le y\le\ln 10$. On the curve, $x=e^y$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=10\ln 10-\int_0^{\ln 10}e^y\,dy \\ &=10\ln 10-\Big[e^y\Big]_0^{\ln 10} \\ &=10\ln 10-(10-1) \\ &=10\ln 10-9 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x$.
Hence, find $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$.
Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x\cos x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x=\sin x+x\cos x$$

Integrate both sides of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int(\sin x+x\cos x)\,dx&=x\sin x \\ \int\sin x\,dx+\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x \\ -\cos x+\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x \\ \int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x+\cos x+C \end{aligned}$$

Using part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi}x\cos x\,dx&=\Big[x\sin x+\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:

$$\int_2^4\dfrac{2x^2-1}{x}\,dx$$

solutions.latex:
Split the integrand into separate terms:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^4\dfrac{2x^2-1}{x}\,dx&=\int_2^4\left(2x-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx\\ &=\Big[x^2-\ln|x|\Big]_2^4\\ &=(4^2-\ln 4)-(2^2-\ln 2)\\ &=12-\ln 4+\ln 2\\ &=12-2\ln 2+\ln 2\\ &=12-\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
(Allow $12+\ln\dfrac{1}{2}$.)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\ln x\right)&=2x\ln x+x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=x+2x\ln x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some attempt to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Rearrange so the integrand uses the derivative from (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\ln x\right)=x+2x\ln x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^e x\ln x\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e 2x\ln x\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\big((2x\ln x+x)-x\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x^2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^e\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(e^2\ln e-\dfrac{e^2}{2}\right)-\left(1\ln 1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{e^2}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{e^2+1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Find the value of $k$ such that the area is 10 square units.

solutions.latex:
For $x\ge 0$, $|x|=x$; for $x<0$, $|x|=-x$:
$$x=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3\quad\text{or}\quad -x=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3$$
Multiply by 2:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=x+6 & -2x&=x+6\\ x&=6 & -3x&=6\\ & & x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Each root satisfies its case ($6\ge 0$, $-2<0$):
$$\therefore\ x=-2,\ 6$$
criteria: One correct solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The region from $x=-2$ to $x=0$ (between the line and $y=-x$):
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=\int_{-2}^0\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x+3-(-x)\right)dx\\ &=\int_{-2}^0\left(\dfrac{3}{2}x+3\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{4}+3x\right]_{-2}^0\\ &=0-\left(\dfrac{3(-2)^2}{4}+3(-2)\right)\\ &=3 \end{aligned}$$
(Or as a triangle, $A_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 2=3$.)

So $7$ square units more are needed for $x$ from $0$ to $k$.

The whole triangle from $x=0$ to $x=6$ has area $\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6=9>7$, so $k<6$.

For $0\le x\le k$, the region lies between the line and $y=x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=\int_0^k\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x+3-x\right)dx\\ 7&=\int_0^k\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3\right)dx\\ 7&=\left[-\dfrac{1}{4}x^2+3x\right]_0^k\\ 7&=-\dfrac{1}{4}k^2+3k\\ k^2-12k+28&=0\\ (k-6)^2&=8\\ k&=6\pm 2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
But $k<6$:
$$\therefore\ k=6-2\sqrt{2}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\sec x + \tan x = \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sec x + \tan x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin x)(1 - \sin x)}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x} = \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Multiplies numerator and denominator by $1 - \sin x$, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions copy (images, no text layer)

solutions.latex:
Using part (a), the numerator $\cos x$ is $-1$ times the derivative of the denominator $1 - \sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}\,dx &= -\Big[\ln|1 - \sin x|\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= -\ln\left|1 - \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right| + \ln|1 - \sin 0| \\ &= -\ln\dfrac{2 - \sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \ln\dfrac{2}{2 - \sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive $-\ln|1 - \sin x|$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right)=e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$$

Hence evaluate

$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)\,dx$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
Then, using $\sec^2 x=\tan^2 x+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right) &= e^x\tan x+e^x\sec^2 x\\ &= e^x\left(\sec^2 x+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+1+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Sets up the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From (a), $e^x\tan x$ is a primitive of $e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)dx &= \Big[e^x\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &= e^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-e^0\tan 0\\ &= \sqrt{3}\,e^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the two curves intersect at the point $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{1+a}},\dfrac{a}{1+a}\right)$.
Find the value of $a$ such that the areas of the two regions are equal.

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} -x^2+1 &= ax^2\\ (a+1)x^2 &= 1\\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{a+1}\\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}} \end{aligned}$$
$x\ge 0$ is given, so $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2\\ &= \dfrac{a}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $y=a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2=\dfrac{a}{a+1}$ (the factor $a$ was missing).

solutions.latex:
Method 1

$S_1+S_2$ is the area under $L_1$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_1+S_2 &= \int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\ &= \left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $S_1=S_2$, so $2S_1=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $S_1=S_2=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$S_1$ lies between $L_1$ (above) and $L_2$ (below), from $x=0$ to the intersection in (a):
$$\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}(-x^2+1-ax^2)\,dx\\ &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\left(1-(1+a)x^2\right)dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{1+a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1+a}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)-0\\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $S_1=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{3}\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^2(1+a)\\ (1+a)^2(1+a)-4(1+a)^2 &= 0\\ (1+a)^2(1+a-4) &= 0\\ a &= -1 \text{ or } a=3 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=3$.

Method 2

$S_2=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx-S_1$ and $S_1=S_2$, so
$$S_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx$$
then continue as in Method 1.

Method 3

From Method 1:
$$S_1=\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}$$
$S_2$ is the area under $L_2$ up to the intersection, plus the area under $L_1$ from the intersection to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_2 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}ax^2\,dx+\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[\dfrac{a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}+\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1\\ &= \dfrac{a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}+\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2+2a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} \end{aligned}$$
Equating $S_1$ and $S_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\\ \dfrac{2(1+a)}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= 1\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^3\\ (1+a)^2(a-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$a=-1$ is outside the domain.
$$\therefore\ a=3$$
criteria: Forms an equation in $a$, such as $\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{1+a}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the primitive for $S_1$, $\left[x-\dfrac{(1+a)x^3}{3}\right]$, or equivalent merit
Writes an integral for $S_1$ with limits $0$ and $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}$, or finds $S_1+S_2=\dfrac{2}{3}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x+4 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left((2x+4)e^x\right)&=e^x\times 2+(2x+4)\times e^x\\ &=e^x\left[2+2x+4\right]\\ &=e^x(2x+6) \end{aligned}$$

$$\int e^x(2x+6)\,dx=(2x+4)e^x+c$$

From part (a):
$$\int\left(2xe^x+6e^x\right)dx=(2x+4)e^x+c$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 2xe^x\,dx&=\Big[(2x+4)e^x\Big]_0^1-\int_0^1 6e^x\,dx\\ &=(2+4)e^1-4e^0-6\Big[e^x\Big]_0^1\\ &=6e-4-6\left[e-1\right]\\ &=6e-4-6e+6\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses part (a) correctly, or equivalent merit

Areas below the x-axis.reason: Signed-area splitting is one method; the direct alternative evaluates the integral without it.

solutions.latex:
For $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(3\sin 2x-3\sin 2a)\,dx=0$, the area below the line $y=3\sin 2a$ (from $0$ to $a$) must equal the area above it (from $a$ to $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$):
$$\int_0^a(3\sin 2a-3\sin 2x)\,dx=\int_a^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(3\sin 2x-3\sin 2a)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[3x\sin 2a-\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2x\right)\right]_0^a&=\left[-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2x-3x\sin 2a\right]_a^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ 3a\sin 2a+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a-\left(0+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 0\right)&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a-\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a-3a\sin 2a\right)\\ 3a\sin 2a+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a-\dfrac{3}{2}&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\times 0-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a+3a\sin 2a\\ -\dfrac{3}{2}&=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a\\ -6&=-3\pi\sin 2a\\ \sin 2a&=\dfrac{6}{3\pi}=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\\ 2a&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)=0.6901070914\\ a&=0.3450535457\\ &=0.345 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative (direct): $3\sin 2a$ is a constant, so
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}3\sin 2x\,dx=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}3\sin 2a\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}&=\Big[3x\sin 2a\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ \dfrac{3}{2}&=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a\\ a&=0.345 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes a correct area statement, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the area $A_1=\dfrac{27}{16}\ \text{u}^2$.
Hence, or otherwise determine the value of $k$.

solutions.latex:
$A_1$ lies above the $x$-axis between $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=\int_0^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(6x^2-4x^3\right)dx\\ &=\Big[2x^3-x^4\Big]_0^{\frac{3}{2}}\\ &=\left[2\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^4\right]-[0]\\ &=\dfrac{27}{4}-\dfrac{81}{16}\\ &=\dfrac{27}{16}\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral with boundaries, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct integral with boundaries; correct showing of all steps to get required answer

solutions.latex:
$A_2$ lies below the $x$-axis, so for $A_2=A_1$ its integral is $-\dfrac{27}{16}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{3}{2}}^{k}\left(6x^2-4x^3\right)dx&=-\dfrac{27}{16}\\ \Big[2x^3-x^4\Big]_{\frac{3}{2}}^{k}&=-\dfrac{27}{16}\\ \left[2k^3-k^4\right]-\left[2\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^4\right]&=-\dfrac{27}{16}\\ 2k^3-k^4-\dfrac{27}{4}+\dfrac{81}{16}&=-\dfrac{27}{16}\\ 2k^3-k^4&=0\\ k^3(2-k)&=0\\ k&=0\text{ or } k=2\end{aligned}$$
Since $k>\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$\therefore k=2$$
Alternatively, the signed areas above and below the axis add to $0$, so solve
$$\int_0^k\left(6x^2-4x^3\right)dx=0$$

parts.latex: The function $y=|x|$ is subjected to the following transformations. For each of the transformations, write the correct equation that arises.
Vertical dilation by a factor of $2$.
Horizontal translation of the equation in part (i) to the left by $1$ unit.
Horizontal dilation of the equation in part (ii) by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Hence or otherwise, find the value of $a$, where $a>0$ such that

$$\int_{-\frac{3}{4}}^{a}\Big(2\,|2x+1|-1\Big)\,dx=0$$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1367_q13_s1}

From part (a)(iii), $y=2|2x+1|-1$ has its vertex at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},-1\right)$ and crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $x=-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

For $-\dfrac{3}{4}\le x\le -\dfrac{1}{2}$ the region is a triangle below the axis, of area
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\times 1=\dfrac{1}{8}$$
From $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $x=0$ the line rises from $-1$ to $1$, so its integral there is $0$.

So the integral from $-\dfrac{3}{4}$ to $a$ is zero when the area above the axis from $0$ to $a$ is $\dfrac{1}{8}$. For $x\ge 0$, $2x+1>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^a\left(2|2x+1|-1\right)dx&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ \int_0^a(4x+1)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ \Big[2x^2+x\Big]_0^a&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ 2a^2+a&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ 16a^2+8a-1&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula, with $a>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{-8\pm\sqrt{8^2+4\times 16}}{2\times 16}\\ &=\dfrac{-8\pm 8\sqrt{2}}{32}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the triangle below the axis for $-\dfrac{3}{4}\le x\le -\dfrac{1}{4}$ has area
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
so the triangle above the axis from $x=-\dfrac{1}{4}$ to $x=a$ (height $2(2a+1)-1$) must also have area $\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(a+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\times\big(2(2a+1)-1\big)&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \left(a+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)(4a+1)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 4a^2+2a+\dfrac{1}{4}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 16a^2+8a-1&=0\end{aligned}$$
and, as above, $a=-\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}$.
criteria: Obtains the correct integral, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the parts below the axis are written as areas (the source set their integrals equal to positive values, e.g. $\displaystyle\int_{-0.75}^{-0.5}=\dfrac{1}{8}$, and jumped to $\displaystyle\int_0^a$ without the zero integral from $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $0$), and the discriminant is $8^2+4\times 16$ (source printed $8^2-4\times 16$).

995.stem:
Two curves $y=2e^{-x}$ and $y=e^x-1$ intersect at point $P$.

\exfigure{1367_q26_1}

figures.cap: curves y = 2e^{-x} and y = e^x - 1 intersecting at P; region between the curves and the y-axis, left of P, shaded

parts.latex: Show that the coordinates of $P$ are $(\ln 2,1)$.
Hence, calculate the shaded area in simplest exact form.

solutions.latex:
At $P$ the curves meet; multiplying by $e^x$ gives a quadratic in $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^x-1&=2e^{-x}\\ e^{2x}-e^x-2&=0\\ \left(e^x-2\right)\left(e^x+1\right)&=0\\ e^x&=-1\text{ or } e^x=2\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^x>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^x&=2\\ x&=\ln 2\\ y&=e^{\ln 2}-1\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore P(\ln 2,1)$$
criteria: Factorises the exponential equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le\ln 2$, $y=2e^{-x}$ lies above $y=e^x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\ln 2}\left(2e^{-x}-e^x+1\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-2e^{-x}-e^x+x\Big]_0^{\ln 2}\\ &=-2e^{-\ln 2}-e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2-\left(-2e^0-e^0+0\right)\\ &=-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-2+\ln 2-(-2-1)\\ &=\ln 2-3+3\\ &=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for the area, or equivalent merit

The diagram below shows the graph of $y=\ln x$. The region bounded by the graph, the $x$-axis and the line $x=7$ has been shaded.

figures.cap: graph of y = ln x with the region under the curve from x = 1 to x = 7 shaded; x-axis ticks 1 to 7

parts.latex: Using the trapezoidal rule with 4 function values, find the approximate shaded area in exact form.
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,(x\ln x)$.
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_1^7\ln x\,dx$.
Deduce that $\ln 7\approx\dfrac{1}{3}\,(\ln 3+\ln 5)+1$.

solutions.latex:
Four function values give three strips:
$$\begin{aligned}h&=\dfrac{7-1}{3}\\ &=2\end{aligned}$$
so $x=1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$:

\extable{Ts1403_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}\left[0+\ln 7+2(\ln 3+\ln 5)\right]\\ &=2\ln 3+2\ln 5+\ln 7\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)&=\ln x+\dfrac{1}{x}\times x\\ &=\ln x+1\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Progress towards the answer, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrating both sides of the result from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^7(\ln x+1)\,dx&=\int_1^7\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)\,dx\\ \int_1^7\ln x\,dx+\int_1^7dx&=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7\\ \int_1^7\ln x\,dx&=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\Big[x\Big]_1^7\\ &=7\ln 7-0-(7-1)\\ &=7\ln 7-6\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates both sides of the equation in part (b), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The trapezoidal estimate in part (a) approximates the integral in part (c), so
$$\begin{aligned}7\ln 7-6&\approx 2\ln 3+2\ln 5+\ln 7\\ 6\ln 7&\approx 2\ln 3+2\ln 5+6\\ \ln 7&\approx\dfrac{1}{3}(\ln 3+\ln 5)+1\end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the relation between parts (a) and (c) is an approximation, written $\approx$ throughout (source wrote $=$ in the first two lines).

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be an even function. It is given that $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{-1}f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{25}{6}$.

Which of the following equals $\displaystyle\int_3^5\big(f(2-x)+f(x-2)\big)\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
$f$ is even, so $f(2-x)=f\big(-(x-2)\big)=f(x-2)$ and the integrand is $2f(x-2)$.

Substituting $u=x-2$, then using the symmetry of the even function $f$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^5 2f(x-2)\,dx&=2\int_1^3 f(u)\,du\\ &=2\int_{-3}^{-1} f(u)\,du\\ &=2\times\dfrac{25}{6}\\ &=\dfrac{25}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A plane is flying through clouds to drop a water quality monitoring system onto a lake.

The lake is surrounded by forest as shown below, with all measurements in metres.

\exfigure{641_q21_1}

Estimate the probability that the plane will drop the monitoring system onto the lake.

Use the Trapezoidal rule in your calculations.

solutions.latex:
The rectangle is 450 m wide and 700 m long.

The centre measurement of the lake is
$$450-70-80=300$$
Using the trapezoidal rule with 2 strips along the 700 m length, $h=\dfrac{700}{2}=350$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of lake}&\approx\dfrac{350}{2}(80+2\times300+100)\\ &=136\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Area of rectangle}=700\times450=315\,000 \text{ m}^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{success})&=\dfrac{\text{Area of lake}}{\text{Area of rectangle}}\\ &=\dfrac{136\,500}{315\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The probability that the monitoring system will drop onto the lake is $\dfrac{13}{30}$, or about $43.3\%$.
criteria: Correctly finds the area of the lake and the rectangle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
By considering $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$, find the exact area enclosed by the curves and the $x$ axis between $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

criteria: Provides a correct equation involving $\tan^2 x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Sketch the two graphs to see the region:

\exfigure{1371_q30_s1}

Points of intersection:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-3&=x+2\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x=5\text{ or }x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
The line $y=x+2$ is above the parabola on $[-1,5]$, so the area is
$$\int_{-1}^{5}(\text{top curve}-\text{bottom curve})\,dx$$

$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-1}^{5}\big((x+2)-(x^2-3x-3)\big)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(x+2-x^2+3x+3)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{5^3}{3}+2(5)^2+5(5)\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\&=36\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $f''(x)<0$ for all positive values of $x$.
Is the answer to part (b) an overestimate or an underestimate? Give a reason for your answer.

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=-e^{-x}-e^x\\f''(x)&=e^{-x}-e^x\end{aligned}$$
As $e^{-x}<e^x$ for all $x>0$:
$$e^{-x}-e^x<0\text{ for all }x>0$$
$\therefore f''(x)<0$ for all $x>0$.

parts.latex:
Show that the volume $V$ of shampoo in the bottle, if it is partially filled to a height of 10 cm, is

$$\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3$$

parts.latex:
The bottle is turned upside down and the entire volume of the shampoo allowed to settle, as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1372_q32_2}

Show that the shampoo level $h$ is given by

$$\left(40\sqrt{5}-10\sqrt{10}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\text{ cm}$$
can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

Area with respect to the y-axis.reason: Method 1 integrates in y, Method 2 integrates in x: one valid method of two.

solutions.latex:
Method 1 (integrating with respect to $y$): from $y=20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$,
$$x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{100-5y}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^{10}\dfrac{\sqrt{100-5y}}{2}\,dy\\&=\int_0^{10}\sqrt{100-5y}\,dy\\&=\left[-\dfrac{2}{15}(100-5y)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^{10}\\&=-\dfrac{2}{15}\left(50^{\frac{3}{2}}-100^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\&=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
The volume of the prism is the cross-sectional area times the width:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=Ah\\&=\left(\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\times4\\&=\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (rectangle plus side regions): at $y=10$,
$$20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2=10\text{, so }x=\pm\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\times\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\times10+2\int_{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{5}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx\\&=50\sqrt{2}+2\left[20x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{5}\\&=50\sqrt{2}+2\left(100-\dfrac{100}{3}-\left(50\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{25}{3}\sqrt{2}\right)\right)\\&=50\sqrt{2}+2\left(\dfrac{200}{3}-\dfrac{125\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
Method 3 (whole parabola minus the unshaded cap):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-5}^{5}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx-\int_{-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2-10\right)dx\\&=\left[20x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{-5}^{5}-\left[10x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}\\&=\left(200-\dfrac{200}{3}\right)-\left(50\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{50\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
In each method:
$$V=4A=\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3$$
criteria: Correct cross-sectional area $\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Method 1: $y=\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{5y}}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^h\dfrac{\sqrt{5y}}{2}\,dy\\&=\sqrt{5}\int_0^h\sqrt{y}\,dy\\&=\sqrt{5}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[y^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^h\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}\left(h^{\frac{3}{2}}-0\right)\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: $h=\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$ gives $x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^{\frac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}}\left(h-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx\\&=2\left[hx-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}}\\&=2\left(h\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}-\dfrac{4}{15}\times\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}\right)^3-(0-0)\right)\\&=\sqrt{5}h^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{\sqrt{5}h^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
The area of the uniform cross-section of shampoo remains the same, so using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}}&=\dfrac{400-100\sqrt{2}}{3}\\h^{\frac{3}{2}}&=\dfrac{400-100\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{5}}\\&=40\sqrt{5}-10\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore h=\left(40\sqrt{5}-10\sqrt{10}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\text{ cm}$$

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)$.
Hence, find $\displaystyle\int xe^{-x}\,dx$.

The diagram below shows the shaded region bounded by the function $y=xe^{-x}$ and the line $y=\dfrac{x}{e}$. By using part (b), find the exact area of the shaded region.

Integrals of exponential functions.reason: Primitive of xe^{-x} is supplied by part (b); no standard exponential primitive used.

Integration using a given derivative.reason: Reversing the derivative was done in part (b); this part only uses that primitive.

Indefinite integrals.reason: Primitive of x/e needed for the area.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)&=1\times e^{-x}+x\times\left(-e^{-x}\right)\\&=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $xe^{-x}=e^{-x}-\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)$.

Hence,
$$\begin{aligned}\int xe^{-x}\,dx&=\int\left(e^{-x}-\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)\right)dx\\&=\int e^{-x}\,dx-xe^{-x}\\&=-e^{-x}-xe^{-x}+c\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The shaded area is the integral of the difference between the curves between their points of intersection; $y=xe^{-x}$ is the upper curve.

To find the points of intersection, equate the two expressions for $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{e}&=xe^{-x}\\ xe^{-1}&=xe^{-x} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $e^{-1}=e^{-x}$, giving $x=1$.

Using the primitive of $xe^{-x}$ from part (b), the shaded area is
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \left(xe^{-x}-\dfrac{x}{e}\right)dx&=\left[-e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-\dfrac{x^2}{2e}\right]_0^1\\ &=\left(-e^{-1}-e^{-1}-\dfrac{1}{2e}\right)-(-1-0-0)\\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{2e} \end{aligned}$$

The curve cuts the $x$-axis where $h(x)=0$:

Region $A$ (below the axis, $0\le x\le\sqrt{2}$) has the same area as region $B$ (above the axis, $\sqrt{2}\le x\le a$):

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-\ln 6}^{\ln 2}\left(-e^{2x}+4-e^x+5\right)dx\\&=\int_{-\ln 6}^{\ln 2}\left(-e^{2x}-e^x+9\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-e^{2x}}{2}-e^x+9x\right]_{-\ln 6}^{\ln 2}\\&=\dfrac{-e^{2\ln 2}}{2}-e^{\ln 2}+9\ln 2-\left(\dfrac{-e^{-2\ln 6}}{2}-e^{-\ln 6}-9\ln 6\right)\\&=\dfrac{-4}{2}-2+9\ln 2-\left(\dfrac{-6^{-2}}{2}-\dfrac{1}{6}-9\ln 6\right)\\&=9\ln 2+9\ln 6-\dfrac{275}{72}\\&=9\ln 12-\dfrac{275}{72}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int\sin ax\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{a}\cos ax+C$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int5\sin2x\,dx&=\dfrac{-5\cos2x}{2}+C\\&=-\dfrac{5}{2}\cos2x+C\end{aligned}$$

Writing the integrand with powers of $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}I&=\int_1^4\left(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}+3x^{-1}\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}+3\ln|x|\right]_1^4\\&=\left[\dfrac{4x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}+3\ln|x|\right]_1^4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}+3\ln4-\left(\dfrac{4}{3}+3\ln1\right)\\&=\dfrac{28}{3}+3\ln4\end{aligned}$$
Since $3\ln 4=\ln 64$, this is also $\dfrac{28}{3}+\ln64$.

parts.latex: Given $y=(\ln x)^2$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2(\ln x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\&=\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\ln x^2=2\ln x$, then part (a): $\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}$ is the derivative of $(\ln x)^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln x^2}{2x}\,dx&=\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{2x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(\ln x)^2\Big]_1^e\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left((\ln e)^2-(\ln1)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1^2-0^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rewrites the integral as $\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows the graphs of the functions $y=2\cos x$ and $y=\cot x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.

\exfigure{165_q13_1}
Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, and solve this equation.
Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)=\cot x$.
Hence, or otherwise, find, in simplest form, the total area of the region enclosed by the two curves for $0\le x\le\pi$.

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where $2\cos x=\cot x$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos x&=\cot x\\2\cos x&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\2\sin x\cos x&=\cos x\\2\sin x\cos x-\cos x&=0\\\cos x(2\sin x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Either $\cos x=0$:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
or $2\sin x-1=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Shows $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$ and finds one pair of solutions, or equivalent merit
Shows $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)&=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\times\cos x\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\end{aligned}$$

For $0\le x\le\pi$ the curves enclose two regions between $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, equal in area by symmetry about $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$.

On $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $2\cos x\ge\cot x$. Using part (b) for the primitive of $\cot x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(2\cos x-\cot x\right)dx\\&=2\Big[2\sin x-\ln(\sin x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=2\left[2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\right]\\&=2\left[2-\ln1-1+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\&=2+2\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=2-2\ln2\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Each rectangle has width 1 and height $p^x$ at its left end ($x=0,1,2,3$):

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{curve}}&=\int_0^4 p^x\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{p^x}{\ln p}\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{p^4}{\ln p}-\dfrac{p^0}{\ln p}\\ &=\dfrac{p^4-1}{\ln p}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} x^3\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
Since $y=x^3$ is an odd function,
$$\int_{-2}^{2}x^3\,dx=0$$
The area under $y=x^3$ from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is above the $x$-axis, so
$$\int_0^2x^3\,dx>0$$
Option A adds an absolute value to this positive integral, and option C doubles it, so both are greater than $0$.

Reversing the limits in option D (and using $x^3$ odd):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2x^3\,dx+\int_0^{-2}x^3\,dx&=\int_0^2x^3\,dx-\int_{-2}^{0}x^3\,dx\\&=2\int_0^2x^3\,dx\end{aligned}$$
which is also greater than $0$.

Since $y^{\frac{1}{3}}$ is also an odd function,
$$\int_{-8}^{8}y^{\frac{1}{3}}\,dy=0$$
so option B is equivalent.

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows a sketch of the curve $C$ with equation

$$y=\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4,\qquad x\ge 0$$

The point $P$ lies on the curve and has $x$-coordinate 4. The line $l$ is the normal to the curve at $P$.

\exfigure{320_q27_1}

Find the exact area of the shaded region $R$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{320_q27_s1}

$R$ is the area under the curve from $x=1$ to $x=4$ plus the triangle under the normal from $P$ to its $x$-intercept.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4\\ &=16x^{-2}+3x-4\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-32x^{-3}+3\end{aligned}$$
At $P(4,9)$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{tangent}}&=-32(4)^{-3}+3\\ &=2.5\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_1m_2=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{normal}}&=-\dfrac{1}{2.5}\\ &=-\dfrac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$$
Equation of normal, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-9&=-\dfrac{2}{5}(x-4)\\ 5y-45&=-2x+8\\ 2x+5y-53&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x$-intercept ($y=0$):
$$\begin{aligned}2x+5(0)-53&=0\\ 2x&=53\\ x&=26.5\end{aligned}$$
The triangle has base $26.5-4=22.5$ and height 9:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_1^4\left(\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4\right)dx+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times22.5\times9\right)\\ &=\int_1^4\left(16x^{-2}+3x-4\right)dx+101.25\\ &=\left[\dfrac{16x^{-1}}{-1}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-4x\right]_1^4+101.25\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{16}{x}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-4x\right]_1^4+101.25\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{16}{4}+\dfrac{3(4)^2}{2}-4(4)\right)-\left(-\dfrac{16}{1}+\dfrac{3(1)^2}{2}-4(1)\right)+101.25\\ &=22.5+101.25\\ &=123.75\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly forms the integral to find the area, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Suppose that $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{8} f(x)\,dx=A$ and $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{8} f(x)\,dx=B$.

The value of $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{-3}\left(f(x)+2x\right)dx$ is:

solutions.latex:
Split the interval at $2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-3}^{8} f(x)\,dx &= \int_{-3}^{2} f(x)\,dx+\int_{2}^{8} f(x)\,dx \\ A &= \int_{-3}^{2} f(x)\,dx+B \\ \int_{-3}^{2} f(x)\,dx &= A-B \end{aligned}$$

Reversing the limits,

$$\int_{2}^{-3} f(x)\,dx=-(A-B)=B-A$$

Then

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{2}^{-3}\left(f(x)+2x\right)dx &= \int_{2}^{-3} f(x)\,dx+\int_{2}^{-3} 2x\,dx \\ &= B-A+\left[x^2\right]_{2}^{-3} \\ &= B-A+9-4 \\ &= B-A+5 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{5x^3-6x^2+3}{x^2}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Divide each term of the numerator by $x^2$, then integrate:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{5x^3-6x^2+3}{x^2}\,dx &= \int_{1}^{3}\left(\dfrac{5x^3}{x^2}-\dfrac{6x^2}{x^2}+\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)dx \\ &= \int_{1}^{3}\left(5x-6+3x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-6x+\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-6x-\dfrac{3}{x}\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \left[\dfrac{5(3)^2}{2}-6(3)-\dfrac{3}{(3)}\right]-\left[\dfrac{5(1)^2}{2}-6(1)-\dfrac{3}{(1)}\right] \\ &= \left[22\dfrac{1}{2}-18-1\right]-\left[2\dfrac{1}{2}-6-3\right] \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)$ and hence show $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C$.
Find the area of the logo. Give your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= \cos x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x$$

Integrate both sides:

$$\begin{aligned} \int(\cos x-x\sin x)\,dx &= x\cos x \\ \int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx &= x\cos x \\ \int x\sin x\,dx &= \int\cos x\,dx-x\cos x \\ &= \sin x-x\cos x+C \end{aligned}$$

Find the intersection points:

$$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= x\sin x \\ \sin x(1-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $\sin x=0$ or $x=1$.

In $0\le x\le\pi$, the curves meet at $x=0,\ 1,\ \pi$.

The intersection at $x=1$ lies between $0$ and $\pi$, so split the area there.

Using part (a), $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx+\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-(\sin x-x\cos x)\Big]_0^1+\Big[(\sin x-x\cos x)+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi} \\ &= (-\cos 1-\sin 1+\cos 1)-(-\cos 0-\sin 0+0)+\Big[(\sin\pi-\pi\cos\pi+\cos\pi)-(\sin 1-\cos 1+\cos 1)\Big] \\ &= (1-\sin 1)+(\pi-1-\sin 1) \\ &= \pi-2\sin 1\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct primitives, or equivalent merit

Finds the intersection points, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x-1 & v &= \sin 2x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= 2\cos 2x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= u'v+uv' \\ &= \sin 2x+(x-1)(2\cos 2x) \\ &= \sin 2x+2(x-1)\cos 2x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x+(x-1)\cos 2x\right)dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sin 2x+2(x-1)\cos 2x\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(x-1)\sin 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-1\right)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-(0-1)\sin 0\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{8}-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Reverse chain rule.reason: Only used to verify option A; not needed for the answer.

Circles and semicircles.reason: Only used to verify option B, not needed to identify D.

solutions.latex:
The question asks for the statement that is not true, so check each option.

The first and third statements are true, using the integral formulas from the reference sheet:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x(x^2-1)^2\,dx&=\dfrac{(x^2-1)^3}{6}+c\\\int_{-1}^{1}3^x\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln3}\right]_{-1}^{1}=\dfrac{8}{3\ln3}\end{aligned}$$
$y=\sqrt{9-x^2}$ is a semicircle of radius 3, so
$$\int_{-3}^{3}\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(3)^2=\dfrac{9\pi}{2}$$
which is also true.

In the last statement, $-x^3$ is odd so it integrates to $0$ over $[-5,5]$, but $4x^4$ and $\cos x$ are even and positive on average, so
$$\int_{-5}^{5}\left(4x^4-x^3+\cos x\right)dx=2\int_{0}^{5}\left(4x^4+\cos x\right)dx\ne0$$
Hence this is the statement that is not true.

$$\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C.$$
Hence, calculate the area (shaded in orange) of the logo, correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Integrate both sides of the given result:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)\,dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx\\x\cos x&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx\\\int x\sin x\,dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-x\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C\quad\text{as required}$$

The curves intersect when
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=x\sin x\\\sin x-x\sin x&=0\\\sin x(1-x)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $\sin x=0$ or $1-x=0$, giving $x=0,\ \pi$ or $x=1$.

As $\sin x>0$ for $0<x<\pi$, the upper curve changes at $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&>x\sin x &&\text{for } 0<x<1\\x\sin x&>\sin x &&\text{for } 1<x<\pi\end{aligned}$$
Using $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx\\&=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1\\&=-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1-(-\cos0-\sin0+0)\\&=1-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=\int_1^\pi(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx\\&=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^\pi\\&=\sin\pi-\pi\cos\pi+\cos\pi-(\sin1-\cos1+\cos1)\\&=-1+\pi-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total shaded area}&=1-\sin1+(-1+\pi-\sin1)\\&=\pi-2\sin1\\&\approx1.46\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{5x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=5e^{5x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{5x}\right)&=e^{5x}+x\cdot5e^{5x}\\&=e^{5x}(5x+1)\end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graphs of y = e^{-x} and y = e^{-x/2} - 1/4 meeting at P, region between them and the y-axis shaded

parts.latex: Show that the point of intersection, $P$, is $\left(\ln 4,\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$.
Hence find the area bounded by the two curves and the $y$-axis, as shaded in the diagram.

solutions.latex:
At the intersection, $e^{-x}=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Multiply both sides by $4e^{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=4e^{\frac{x}{2}}-e^{x}\\e^{x}-4e^{\frac{x}{2}}+4&=0\\\left(e^{\frac{x}{2}}-2\right)^2&=0\\e^{\frac{x}{2}}&=2\\\dfrac{x}{2}&=\ln2\\x&=\ln4\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into $y=e^{-x}$:
$$y=e^{-\ln4}=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
So $P$ is $\left(\ln4,\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$.

meta.top_criterion_original: clear working (substitution method allowed). Common mistake: $\ln\dfrac{1}{4}=\ln e^{-x}-\ln e^{-\frac{x}{2}}$.
meta.marker_note: Clear working is required (substitution method allowed). Common mistake: $\ln\dfrac{1}{4}=\ln e^{-x}-\ln e^{-\frac{x}{2}}$.

solutions.latex:
Between $x=0$ (the $y$-axis) and $x=\ln4$ (point $P$), $y=e^{-x}$ is the upper curve:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\ln4}\left(e^{-x}-e^{-\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dx\\&=\left[-e^{-x}+2e^{-\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{x}{4}\right]_0^{\ln4}\\&=-e^{-\ln4}+2e^{-\frac{\ln4}{2}}+\dfrac{\ln4}{4}-(-1+2+0)\\&=-\dfrac{1}{4}+1+\dfrac{\ln4}{4}-1\\&=\dfrac{\ln4-1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{\ln4-1}{4}\text{ units}^2\ (\approx0.097)$$

parts.latex:
A function $f(x)$ is such that

$$\int_{-k}^{k}f(x)\,dx=2\int_{0}^{k}f(x)\,dx$$

Which of the following could $f(x)$ be?

solutions.latex:
The condition is
$$\int_{-k}^{k}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^k f(x)\,dx$$
This holds when $f$ is an even function, $f(-x)=f(x)$, because the areas on either side of the $y$-axis are equal.

$\cos 2x$ is even, whereas $\sin 2x$, $\tan 2x$ and $\operatorname{cosec}2x$ are odd.

So $f(x)=\cos 2x$ is the function that could satisfy the condition.

parts.latex: If the red area is three times larger than the blue area, find the value of $n$.

solutions.latex:
Let $B$ be the area of the blue region, $W$ the area of the small rectangle and $A$ the area of the big rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned} B&=\int_a^b x^n\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left[x^{n+1}\right]_a^b \\ &=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} W&=a\times a^n \\ &=a^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=b\times b^n \\ &=b^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
The big rectangle is made up of the blue region, the red region ($3B$) and the small rectangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=B+3B+W \\ &=4B+W \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} b^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right)+a^{n+1} \\ b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right) \\ 1&=\dfrac{4}{n+1} \\ 4&=n+1 \\ n&=3 \end{aligned}$$

1746.stem: The function $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ is shown below. It is an odd function.

figures.cap: Graph of y = x/(x^2+1) and line y = mx through the origin with the two enclosed regions shaded

parts.latex:
For what values of $m$ do the line $y=mx$ and the curve $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ enclose a region?

\exfigure{377_q31_1}
can_use: Discriminant and the nature of roots

parts.latex: Find the area of the region (in terms of $m$).

Integrals of odd and even functions.evidence: both odd, so the shaded area is twice the area for x>=0

solutions.latex:
For a region, the line and curve must meet at $3$ points.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{x^2+1} &= mx \\ x &= mx^3+mx \\ mx^3+(m-1)x &= 0 \\ x\big(mx^2+(m-1)\big) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
One solution is $x=0$.

The other two need $x^2=\dfrac{1-m}{m}=\dfrac{1}{m}-1$, so $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{m}-1}$.

For two solutions:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{m}-1 &> 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{m} &> 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<m<1$$
Alternatively, $mx^2+(m-1)=0$ needs a positive discriminant.
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta=-4m(m-1) &> 0 \\ 4m(m-1) &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<m<1$$

Both $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ and $y=mx$ are odd, so the shaded area is twice the area for $x\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\times\int_0^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}-1}}\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}-mx\right)dx \\ &= 2\times\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|x^2+1|-\dfrac{mx^2}{2}\right]_0^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}-1}} \\ &= \ln\left|\dfrac{1}{m}-1+1\right|-m\left(\dfrac{1}{m}-1\right)-(\ln 1-0) \\ &= \ln\left|\dfrac{1}{m}\right|+m-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\ln\left|\dfrac{1}{m}\right|+m-1 \text{ u}^2$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit
Writes the correct integral using symmetry, or equivalent merit

(Hint: show that the function $f(x)=e^x-(1+x)$ is increasing for $x\ge 0$.)
Deduce that $\displaystyle\dfrac{4}{3}\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le e$

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x)=e^x-1-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= e^0-1-0=0 \\ f'(x) &= e^x-1>0 \text{ for } x>0 \end{aligned}$$
So $f(x)$ is increasing for $x\ge 0$ and $f(0)=0$, hence $f(x)\ge 0$ for $x\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x-1-x &\ge 0 \\ e^x &\ge 1+x \end{aligned}$$

For $0\le x\le 1$ we have $x^2\le x$, so $e^{x^2}\le e^x$ (as $e^x$ is increasing).

Using (i) with $x^2$ in place of $x$:
$$1+x^2\le e^{x^2}\le e^x$$
Integrate over $0\le x\le 1$.
$$\int_0^1(1+x^2)\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^x\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[x+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 &\le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le \Big[e^x\Big]_0^1 \\ \left(1+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-0 &\le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le e^1-e^0 \\ \dfrac{4}{3} &\le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le e-1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e-1<e$:
$$\dfrac{4}{3}\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le e$$
criteria: Integrates the inequality, or equivalent merit
Shows $1+x^2\le e^{x^2}\le e^x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Let $f(x)$ be an even function. If $\displaystyle\int_0^6 f(x)\,dx=12$ and $\displaystyle\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx=-5$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4} 2f(x)\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Split the integral from $0$ to $6$ at $4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx &= \int_0^6 f(x)\,dx-\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 12-(-5) \\ &= 17 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{4}2f(x)\,dx &= 2\int_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times 2\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times 2\times 17 \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{mx}\right)$.
Hence find $\displaystyle\int xe^{mx}\,dx$.

The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=xe^{mx}$, the $x$-axis and $x=1$ is shown below. Given that the area of this area is $\dfrac{1}{m}$, find $m$.

\exfigure{382_q32_1}

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{mx}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=me^{mx}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{mx}\right) &= 1\cdot e^{mx}+x\cdot me^{mx} \\ &= e^{mx}+mxe^{mx} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate both sides of the result of part (a) with respect to $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} xe^{mx} &= \int\left(e^{mx}+mxe^{mx}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{m}e^{mx}+m\int xe^{mx}\,dx \end{aligned}$$
Make the integral the subject (the constant of integration is added at the end):
$$\begin{aligned} m\int xe^{mx}\,dx &= xe^{mx}-\dfrac{1}{m}e^{mx} \\ \int xe^{mx}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{m}e^{mx}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates both sides, or work of equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve passes through the origin, so the region runs from $x=0$ to $x=1$. Using part (b), with area $\dfrac{1}{m}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^1 xe^{mx}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{m} \\ \dfrac{1}{m}\left[e^{mx}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)\right]_0^1 &= \dfrac{1}{m} \\ e^m\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)-e^0\left(0-\dfrac{1}{m}\right) &= 1 &&(\text{multiply by }m) \\ e^m\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)+\dfrac{1}{m}-1 &= 0 \\ e^m\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)-\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right) &= 0 \\ \left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)\left(e^m-1\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $1-\dfrac{1}{m}=0$ or $e^m=1$, giving $m=1$ or $m=0$. But $m\ne 0$, since the area is $\dfrac{1}{m}$.
$$\therefore\ m=1$$

Between the intersections the parabola is above $y=|x|$, and the region is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\int_0^1 \big((2-x^2)-x\big)\,dx \\ &= 2\left[2x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 \\ &= 2\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7}{3}\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the area is $\dfrac{7}{3}$ units$^2$.

figures.cap: graph of y=x^2-1 from x=0 to x=k with the region below the axis and the region above the axis shaded

solutions.latex:
The two shaded areas are equal, so over $0\le x\le k$ the area below the $x$-axis cancels the area above it, and the integral is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\left(x^2-1\right)dx &= 0 \\ \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_0^k &= 0 \\ \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k &= 0 \\ k^3-3k &= 0 \\ k\left(k^2-3\right) &= 0 \\ k &= 0,\ \pm\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $k>1$, so $k=0$ and $k=-\sqrt{3}$ are rejected.
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt{3}$$
Alternative solution: the area below the axis, from $0$ to $1$, equals the area above it, from $1$ to $k$:
$$\begin{aligned} \left|\int_0^1\left(x^2-1\right)dx\right| &= \int_1^k\left(x^2-1\right)dx \\ \left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_0^1\right| &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_1^k \\ \left|\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right| &= \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right) \\ \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k+\dfrac{2}{3} \\ \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
This is the same equation as before, so $k=\sqrt{3}$.
criteria: Writes a correct equation involving integrals, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A landscaper, Annabel, wanted to ask the local council to renovate the park near her home. Her suggestion was to have a park partially occupied by a lake and the rest be a grassed section, as shown in the diagram below.

solutions.latex:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule means 3 function values, so $h=\dfrac{220}{2}=110$ m. The heights of the grassed section are $135$, $120$ and $180$ m (the right end reaches the top of the rectangle).
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{grass}} &\approx \dfrac{110}{2}\big[135+2(120)+180\big] \\ &= 55\times 555 \\ &= 30\,525 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The rectangle has area $220\times 180=39\,600\text{ m}^2$, so the lake inside the rectangle is
$$39\,600-30\,525=9075\text{ m}^2$$
The semicircle (radius $110$ m) has area
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(110)^2=6050\pi\approx 19\,006.6\text{ m}^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lake} &\approx 9075+19\,006.6 \\ &\approx 28\,082 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Determine the area of the region enclosed by $y^2=2x+6$ and $y=x-1$.
can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $(x-1)^2=2x+6$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-2x+1&=2x+6\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=-1$ or $x=5$, giving the points $(-1,-2)$ and $(5,4)$.

Method 1 (integrate with respect to $x$). From $x=-3$ to $x=-1$ the region lies between $y=-\sqrt{2x+6}$ and $y=\sqrt{2x+6}$. From $x=-1$ to $x=5$ it lies between the line and $y=\sqrt{2x+6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_{-3}^{-1}(2x+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}dx+\int_{-1}^{5}\left((2x+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}-x+1\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(2x+6)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{-3}^{-1}+\left[\dfrac{1}{3}(2x+6)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{2}{3}(0)\right]+\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(16)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{25}{2}+5\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}-1\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{16}{3}+\dfrac{38}{3}\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (integrate with respect to $y$). The line is $x=y+1$ and the parabola is $x=\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3$; between $y=-2$ and $y=4$ the line is to the right of the parabola.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-2}^{4}\left((y+1)-\left(\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3\right)\right)dy\\ &=\int_{-2}^{4}\left(y-\dfrac{y^2}{2}+4\right)dy\\ &=\left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}-\dfrac{y^3}{6}+4y\right]_{-2}^{4}\\ &=\left(8-\dfrac{32}{3}+16\right)-\left(2+\dfrac{4}{3}-8\right)\\ &=\dfrac{40}{3}+\dfrac{14}{3}\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is }18\text{ units}^2$$

parts.latex: Verify, by substitution, that the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},2\right)$ lies on both $y=\sec^2 x$ and $y=2\cot x$.
Differentiate $\ln(\sin x)$.

solutions.latex:
For $y=\sec^2 x$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sec^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
For $y=2\cot x$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{1} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Both give $y=2$, so $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},2\right)$ lies on both curves.
criteria: Verifies one curve, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x) &= \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= \cot x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curves meet at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. The upper boundary of the region is $y=\sec^2 x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $y=2\cot x$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sec^2 x\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\cot x\,dx$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)=\cot x$ from part (ii):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+2\Big[\ln(\sin x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan 0+2\left[\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] \\ &= 1-0+2\left[\ln 1-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right] \\ &= 1+2\left[0-\ln 2^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right] \\ &= 1+\ln 2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Second integral was $\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\cot x\,dx$ (curve $y=\cot x$), giving $1+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2$; the curve is $y=2\cot x$, so it is now $\int 2\cot x\,dx$ and the area is $1+\ln 2$.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the second integral omitted the factor 2 of $y=2\cot x$; the area is $1+\ln 2$, not $1+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2$.

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

These graphs are shown in the diagram below, in which the measurements in the $x$ and $y$ directions are in metres.

parts.latex: The total area of the shaded regions, in squares metres, can be calculated as $a\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin(x)\,dx$. What is the value of $a$?

The coffee company considers changing the functions used in the design of the logo.

Its next attempt used the graphs of the functions,

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ h(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

On the axes below, the graph of $y=f(x)$ has been drawn.

On the same axes, draw the graph of $y=h(x)$.

\exfigure{161_q13_2}
State a sequence of two transformations that maps the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the graph of $y=h(x)$.

The coffee company now considers using the graphs of the functions $k(x)=m\sin(x)$ and $q(x)=\dfrac{1}{n}\sin(n(x))$, where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers with $m\ge 2$ and $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

Give a simplified expression for the area enclosed by the graphs of $y=k(x)$ and $y=q(x)$ in terms of $m$ and $n$ \textbf{if} $\boldsymbol{n}$ \textbf{is even.}

Find the area enclosed by the graphs of $y=k(x)$ and $y=q(x)$ in terms of $m$ and $n$ \textbf{if} $\boldsymbol{n}$ \textbf{is odd.}

Give your answer in the form $am+\dfrac{b}{n^2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

solutions.latex:
By the symmetry of the graphs about $(\pi,0)$, the two shaded regions have equal area.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(2\sin x-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right)dx \end{aligned}$$
Since $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}2\sin x\,dx \\ &= 4\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=4$

meta.format_note: Reasons added to the source's two-line working. Checked numerically: total shaded area $=8=4\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx$.

Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{6}$:
$$2\sin x\ \text{becomes}\ \dfrac{2}{6}\sin x=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin x$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ replaces $x$ by $3x$:
$$\dfrac{1}{3}\sin x\ \text{becomes}\ \dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x$$

solutions.latex:
Both graphs have the same shape each side of $x=\pi$, so the area is twice the area for $0\le x\le\pi$. For even $n$, $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}m\sin x\,dx \\ &= 2m\Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2m\left(-\cos\pi+\cos 0\right) \\ &= 2m(1+1) \\ &= 4m \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Checked numerically ($m=3$, $n=4$: area $12$).

solutions.latex:
For odd $n$, $\cos(n\pi)=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(m\sin x-\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\right)dx \\ &= 2\left[-m\cos x+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos nx\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left\{\left(-m\cos\pi+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos n\pi\right)-\left(-m\cos 0+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos 0\right)\right\} \\ &= 2\left\{\left(m-\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)-\left(-m+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)\right\} \\ &= 2\left\{2m-\dfrac{2}{n^2}\right\} \\ &= 4m-\dfrac{4}{n^2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=4$ and $b=-4$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution, or equivalent merit
