5351.stem:
Let $f(x) = 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ for $x \ge 0$. A right-angled triangle $OQP$ has vertex $O$ at the origin, vertex $Q$ on the $x$-axis and vertex $P$ on the graph of $f(x)$, as shown. The coordinates of $P$ are $(x, f(x))$.

\exfigure{1279_q31_1}

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with triangle OQP shaded
graph of y=f(x) with region between curve and chord ST shaded

parts.latex: Find the area, $A$, of the triangle $OPQ$ in terms of $x$.
Find the maximum area of triangle $OQP$ and the value of $x$ for which the maximum occurs.

Let $S$ be the point on the graph of $f(x)$ on the $y$-axis and let $T$ be the point on the graph of $f(x)$ with the $y$-coordinate $\dfrac{1}{2}$. Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of $f(x)$ and the line segment $ST$.

\exfigure{1279_q31_2}

solutions.latex:
The triangle has base $x$ and height $f(x) = 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times x \times 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ &= xe^{-\frac{x}{5}} \end{aligned}$$

meta.edited_from_original: The question total was recorded as 8 marks while its parts carry 1 + 3 + 5 = 9; the total is now 9 marks (checker flag 24 Nov).

solutions.latex:
A maximum occurs where $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$ and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= -\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= x\left(-\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\right) + e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ &= e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{5}\right) = 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-\frac{x}{5}} > 0$ for all $x$, $x = 5$.

Second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} - \dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} + \dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} = e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\left(\dfrac{x}{25}-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$$
At $x = 5$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = e^{-1}\left(\dfrac15-\dfrac25\right) = -\dfrac{1}{5e} < 0$, so this is a maximum.

At $x = 5$:
$$A = 5e^{-1}$$
$$\therefore\ A_{\max} = \dfrac{5}{e} \text{ units}^2 \text{ at } x = 5$$
criteria: Finds $x=5$ and the maximum area, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the second derivative had $-\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ instead of $+\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$, so "every term is negative" was false; $A^{\prime\prime}(5)=-\dfrac{1}{5e}<0$ still gives a maximum.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the second derivative had $-\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ instead of $+\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$, so "every term is negative" was false; $A^{\prime\prime}(5)=-\dfrac{1}{5e}<0$ still gives a maximum.

solutions.latex:
Find $S$: $f(0) = 2$, so $S(0, 2)$.

Find $T$: solve $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ e^{-\frac{x}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ x &= -5\ln\dfrac{1}{4} = 5\ln 4 \end{aligned}$$
So $T\left(5\ln 4, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

The region lies between the chord $ST$ (above) and the curve (below) for $0 \le x \le 5\ln 4$. Its area is the trapezium under $ST$ (parallel sides $2$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$, width $5\ln 4$) minus the area under the curve.

Trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 5\ln 4\left(2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 \end{aligned}$$
Area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \displaystyle\int_0^{5\ln 4} 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\,dx \\ &= \Big[-10e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\Big]_0^{5\ln 4} \\ &= -10e^{-\ln 4} + 10 \\ &= -10\times\dfrac{1}{4} + 10 \\ &= \dfrac{15}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Required area:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= A_1 - A_2 \\ &= \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 - \dfrac{15}{2} \\ &\approx 1.16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A = \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 - \dfrac{15}{2} \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct integral and trapezium area, or equivalent merit
Correct area expression, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: The area working ran the trapezium and the integral together in one chain, using undefined $h$, $a$, $b$ and skipping the antiderivative ($-\int = +10[e^{-x/5}]$); it now finds the trapezium area $\dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4$ and the area under the curve $\dfrac{15}{2}$ separately, then subtracts. Answer $\dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4-\dfrac{15}{2}\approx1.16$ units$^2$ unchanged (checker flag 24 Nov).

The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x=2$ and $x=4$, so the area is split at $x=2$. The region from $2$ to $4$ lies below the axis, so its integral is made positive.

For what value of $k$ will the area to the left of point $P$ be equal to the area to the right of $P$?

solutions.latex:
The areas left and right of $P$ are equal when
$$\int_0^1\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-x\right)dx=\int_1^k\left(x-x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)dx$$
$$\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_1^k$$
$$\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{k^2}{2}-\dfrac{2k^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{k^2}{2}-\dfrac{2k^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}=0$$
$$k^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\dfrac{k^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2}-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=0$$
Since $k>1$, $k^{\frac{3}{2}}\ne 0$, so $\sqrt{k}=\dfrac{4}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Equates the two areas as integrals, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2} \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write the integrand as a power of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2}\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx&=\displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2}x^{-2}\,dx\\ &=\left[-x^{-1}\right]_{0.5}^{2}\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{0.5}^{2}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}+2\\ &=1\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=4$ into each function.
$$\begin{aligned} f(4)&=\dfrac{4}{2}(4-2)=4\\ g(4)&=2\sqrt{4}=4\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(4)=g(4)$, the graphs meet where $x=4$, so the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $4$.

Between $x=0$ and $x=4$ the curve $g$ is above $f$, so the integrand is $g(x)-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sqrt{x}-\dfrac{x}{2}(x-2)&=2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}+x\end{aligned}$$
The area is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\left(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}+x\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{4}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{6}x^{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}\right]_{0}^{4}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\cdot 8-\dfrac{1}{6}\cdot 64+8\right)-0\\ &=8\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Use the Trapezoidal Rule with 5 function values to find an approximation for the definite integral

$$\int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx .$$
If $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ then $y'' = \dfrac{2}{x^{3}}$. Briefly explain how this implies that your approximation found in part (a) overestimates the exact value of the definite integral.

solutions.latex:
Five function values give four strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{3-1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
and the $x$ values are $1,\ \dfrac{3}{2},\ 2,\ \dfrac{5}{2},\ 3$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} x & 1 & \dfrac{3}{2} & 2 & \dfrac{5}{2} & 3 \\ \hline f(x) & 1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{array}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f_0+2(f_1+f_2+f_3)+f_4\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{1}{4}\left[1+2\left(\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+\dfrac{1}{3}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{67}{15}\\ &=\dfrac{67}{60}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct function values, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equations $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ and $y=11-x$ simultaneously and show that there is one point of intersection. Give its coordinates.

Sketch $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ and $y=11-x$ on the axes below.

Calculate the area bounded by the curves $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ and $y=11-x$ and the $x$-axis.
can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

solutions.latex:
Set the two expressions for $y$ equal and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x+1}&=11-x \\ x+1&=(11-x)^2 \\ x+1&=121-22x+x^2 \\ x^2-23x+120&=0 \\ (x-8)(x-15)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=8$ or $x=15$.

When $x=8$, $y=3$. When $x=15$, $y=-4$.

The radical sign means the positive square root, so $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ is never negative. Hence $(15,-4)$ is not a solution.

The only point of intersection is $(8,3)$.
criteria: Gives both solutions with no explanation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curves meet at $(8,3)$. The area is under $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ from $x=-1$ to $x=8$, then under $y=11-x$ from $x=8$ to $x=11$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-1}^{8}(x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx+\int_8^{11}(11-x)\,dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{2(x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{8}+\left[11x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_8^{11} \\ &=\left[\dfrac{2(9)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-0\right]+\left[\left(121-\dfrac{121}{2}\right)-\left(88-\dfrac{64}{2}\right)\right] \\ &=18+4.5 \\ &=22.5 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The graph is above the $x$-axis for $-1<x<0$ and below it for $0<x<1$.

Since $f$ is odd, the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin, so the two shaded regions have equal area.

On $-1\le x\le 0$ the curve is above the axis, so this area is
$$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}\left(x^3-x\right)dx$$
The total shaded area is twice this.
$$2\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}\left(x^3-x\right)dx$$
Options B, C and D all involve $\displaystyle\int_0^1$ or $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1$. These are negative or zero, since the region on $[0,1]$ is below the axis and the integral over $[-1,1]$ is $0$. So the answer is option A.

Expand the factorised form.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-(x^2-4)(x-1)\\ &=-(x^3-x^2-4x+4) \end{aligned}$$
The curve lies below the $x$-axis for $-2\le x\le 1$ and above it for $1\le x\le 2$, so the area uses the negative of the signed area on $[-2,1]$.

$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{71}{6}\text{ units}^2$$

parts.latex: Show that the curves intersect when $4e^{2x}-5e^x+1=0$.
Show that the points of intersection occur at $x=0$ and $x=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}$.
Hence find the area of the region bounded by $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, correct to three decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Equate $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}4e^x-3&=2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}\\ 4e^{2x}-3e^x&=2e^x-1 &&(\text{multiply by } e^x)\\ 4e^{2x}-5e^x+1&=0\end{aligned}$$

Factorise the quadratic in $e^x$.
$$(4e^x-1)(e^x-1)=0$$
So $e^x=\dfrac{1}{4}$ or $e^x=1$.

Hence $x=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}$ or $x=0$.

From the graph, $f(x)$ is above $g(x)$ between the intersections.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\left[\left(2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}\right)-(4e^x-3)\right]dx\\&=\int_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\left(5-e^{-x}-4e^x\right)dx\\&=\left[5x+e^{-x}-4e^x\right]_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\\&=\left(0+e^0-4e^0\right)-\left(5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}+e^{-\ln\frac{1}{4}}-4e^{\ln\frac{1}{4}}\right)\\&=(-3)-\left(5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}+4-1\right)\\&=-5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}-6\\&=5\ln 4-6\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A\approx 0.931 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Significant progress in finding the area, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show, using any appropriate method, that $B$ has coordinates $\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
Find the exact area of the shaded region.

solutions.latex:
At $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$:
$$\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} &= \sqrt{3}\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So both curves pass through $\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

Alternatively, $\sin x=\sqrt{3}\cos x$ gives $\tan x=\sqrt{3}$, so $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

The second intersection has $x>\pi$, so $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $y=\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

meta.format_note: Source said 'But $x>4$'; read as $x>\pi$ (second intersection) and corrected here.

solutions.latex:
The shaded region lies below the $x$-axis, so each integral is taken in absolute value:
$$\text{Area}=\left|\int_{\pi}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\sin x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_{\frac{4\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}\sqrt{3}\cos x\,dx\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \left|\Big[-\cos x\Big]_{\pi}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\right|+\left|\Big[\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{4\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{2}+(-1)\right|+\left|-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\left|-\sqrt{3}+\dfrac{3}{2}\right| \end{aligned}$$
As $\sqrt{3}>\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &= \sqrt{3}-1 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Both integrals set up and evaluated, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\tan^2 x+\sin 2x\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\tan^2x+\sin2x\right)dx &=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sec^2x-1+\sin2x\right)dx \\ &=\left[\tan x-x-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(\tan0-0-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos0\right) \\ &=\left(1-\dfrac{\pi}{4}-0\right)-\left(0-0-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $\sin^2 x$
Hence calculate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} (\sin x + \cos x)^2\,dx$ , (Leave your answer in exact form.)

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} y&=\sin^2 x \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\cos x\sin x \end{aligned}$$

Expand the integrand and use $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\sin x+\cos x)^2\,dx &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sin^2 x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2 x\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(1+2\sin x\cos x\right)dx \end{aligned}$$
By part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^2 x\right)=2\sin x\cos x$, so

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{1}{1 - \sin x} + \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin x} \equiv 2\sec^2 x$ where $\sin x \ne \pm 1$

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator, then use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x} \\ &=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)+(1-\sin x)}{1-\sin^2 x} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x} \\ &=2\sec^2 x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

The area between the curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve. Using part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}-\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\right)dx \\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}2\sec^2 x\,dx \\ &=2\Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=2\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-0\right) \\ &=2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Simplifies the integrand using part (i), or equivalent merit

The graph below shows the cubic curve $y = 9x - x^3$, with domain $[0, 4.5]$.

\exfigure{1284_q36_1}

The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

The diagram shows two bounded regions:

$R$ bounded by $y = f(x),\ y = 0,\ x = 0$ and $x = 3$

$S$ bounded by $y = f(x),\ y = 0,\ x = 3$ and $x = a$

It is given that $a > 3$. Determine the value of $a$ such that regions $R$ and $S$ have the same area.

solutions.latex:
Region $R$ lies above the $x$-axis and region $S$ lies below it (the curve is negative for $x>3$). Equal areas mean the signed integrals cancel:
$$\int_0^3\left(9x-x^3\right)dx+\int_3^a\left(9x-x^3\right)dx=0$$
The two integrals combine into one:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\left(9x-x^3\right)dx&=0 \\ \left[\dfrac{9x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^a&=0 \\ \dfrac{9a^2}{2}-\dfrac{a^4}{4}&=0 \\ 18a^2-a^4&=0 \\ a^2\left(18-a^2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $a=0$ or $a=\pm 3\sqrt{2}$.

Since $a>3$, we take the positive root:
$$a=3\sqrt{2}$$

parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)$ is $\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$ .
Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{5}{2}$ .

solutions.latex:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(3+x)-\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(3-x) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3+x}-\dfrac{-1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{3-x+3+x}{(3+x)(3-x)} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Splits the log and differentiates correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{6}\int_1^2\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\ln\dfrac{5}{1}-\ln\dfrac{4}{2}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}(\ln 5-\ln 2) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$$

A company's new logo is the region bounded by $y=\sin x$ and $y=x\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. This region is shown shaded in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1295_q32_1}

Calculate the area of the logo, correct to $2$ decimal places.

You may wish to assume the result

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\cos x\right)=\cos x-x\sin x.$$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1295_q32_s1}

From the hint, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x$. Integrating both sides,
$$x\cos x=\sin x-\int x\sin x\,dx$$
$$\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$$
The curves meet where $x\sin x=\sin x$, that is $x=1$ (for $0<x<\pi$). For $0<x<1$, $\sin x>x\sin x$; for $1<x<\pi$, $x\sin x>\sin x$.

First region:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1\\ &=(-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1)-(-1)\\ &=1-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
Second region:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi}\\ &=(\pi-1)-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
Total area:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=A_1+A_2\\ &=1-\sin1+\pi-1-\sin1\\ &=\pi-2\sin1\\ &\approx1.46 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct antiderivative and evaluation of both regions, or equivalent merit
Correct integrals for both regions, or equivalent merit
Splits the area at the intersection, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's total line wrote '1-sin1+π-sin1-1'; the working gives A2=(π-1)-sin1 so the total line was written as 1-sin1+π-1-sin1 (same value π-2sin1).

5847.stem:
The diagram below shows the graph of $y=x^2-2x-8$

\exfigure{1297_q26_1}

figures.cap: graph of y=x^2-2x-8 with A on x-axis and line x=6

parts.latex: What are the coordinates of $A$?
Find the area bounded by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=x^2-2x-8$ between $0\le x\le 6$

solutions.latex:
The curve crosses the $x$-axis where $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-2x-8 &= 0 \\ (x-4)(x+2) &= 0 \\ x &= 4 \text{ or } x=-2 \end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, $A$ is the positive intercept.
$$\therefore\ A=(4,0)$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le 4$ and above it for $4\le x\le 6$, so the two areas are found separately.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 (x^2-2x-8)\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2-8x\right]_0^4 \\ &= -\dfrac{80}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_4^6 (x^2-2x-8)\,dx &= -12-\left(-\dfrac{80}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{44}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left|-\dfrac{80}{3}\right|+\dfrac{44}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{124}{3} \\ &= 41\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds both integrals, or equivalent merit
Finds the primitive, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Primitive and value $\dfrac{44}{3}$ written out; they agree with the source total.

figures.cap: graphs of y=9x and y=x^3-9x with shaded region between 0 and K

parts.latex: By solving the two equations simultaneously, show that $K=3\sqrt{2}$
Hence find the shaded area in the diagram above.

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-9x &= 9x \\ x^3-18x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-18) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x^2=18$, giving $x=\pm\sqrt{18}=\pm3\sqrt{2}$.

Since $K>0$, we have $K=3\sqrt{2}$.
criteria: Equates the two functions and factorises, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The line $y=9x$ lies above the cubic between $x=0$ and $x=3\sqrt{2}$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{3\sqrt{2}}\left[9x-(x^3-9x)\right]dx \\ &= \int_0^{3\sqrt{2}}(18x-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \left[9x^2-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{3\sqrt{2}} \\ &= 162-81 \\ &= 81 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit
Sets up the correct integral, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) on [-1,4] with endpoints (-1,3) and (4,3)

solutions.latex:
Split the integral and integrate the constant.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{4}[f(x)+4]\,dx &= \int_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,dx+\int_{-1}^{4}4\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{15}{2}+\left[4x\right]_{-1}^{4} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{2}+\left[16-4(-1)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{15}{2}+20 \\ &= 27.5 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Splits the integral, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: odd piecewise-linear function with shaded area between x=-2a and x=2a

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the shaded area to the right of the $y$-axis is a triangle (base $a$, height $2a$) and a rectangle ($a$ by $2a$):
$$\int_0^{2a} f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\times a\times 2a+a\times 2a=3a^2$$
The function $f(x)$ is odd, so the shaded area is $2\times 3a^2=6a^2$, but the integral over the symmetric interval is zero:
$$\int_{-2a}^{2a} f(x)\,dx=0$$
This gives a signed area of $0$, not the shaded area. The other options all give $6a^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{B: } 2\displaystyle\int_0^{-2a} f(x)\,dx &= -2\displaystyle\int_{-2a}^{0} f(x)\,dx = -2\left(-3a^2\right) = 6a^2 \\ \text{C: } 2\displaystyle\int_0^{a} f(x)\,dx+4a^2 &= 2a^2+4a^2 = 6a^2 \\ \text{D: } 3(a\times 2a) &= 6a^2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence option A.

meta.edited_from_original: The paper printed option B as $-2\displaystyle\int_0^{-2a} f(x)\,dx$, which equals $-6a^2$ and so also does not give the shaded area (two answers). Option B is now $2\displaystyle\int_0^{-2a} f(x)\,dx=6a^2$, so A is the only answer (checker flag 24 Nov).

figures.cap: region between parabola y^2=2x+6 and line y=x-1

solutions.latex:
Write both curves with $x$ in terms of $y$:
$$x=\dfrac{y^2-6}{2},\qquad x=y+1$$
Intersection:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y^2-6}{2}&=y+1 \\ y^2-6&=2y+2 \\ y^2-2y-8&=0 \\ (y-4)(y+2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $y=4$ or $y=-2$, giving points $(-1,-2)$ and $(5,4)$.

Integrating with respect to $y$, the line is to the right of the parabola:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-2}^{4}\left[(y+1)-\dfrac{y^2-6}{2}\right]dy \\ &=\int_{-2}^{4}\left(-\dfrac{y^2}{2}+y+4\right)dy \\ &=\left[-\dfrac{y^3}{6}+\dfrac{y^2}{2}+4y\right]_{-2}^{4} \\ &=\left[-\dfrac{4^3}{6}+\dfrac{4^2}{2}+4(4)\right]-\left[-\dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}+\dfrac{(-2)^2}{2}+4(-2)\right] \\ &=\dfrac{40}{3}-\left(-\dfrac{14}{3}\right) \\ &=18 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct integral for the shaded area, or equivalent merit
Finds the points of intersection, or equivalent merit

5933.stem:
The graphs of $y=kx$ and $y=12x-x^2$ intersect at the origin and point P. The coordinates of point P are $(8,32)$.

\exfigure{1772_q24_1}

figures.cap: line y=kx and parabola y=12x-x^2 intersecting at origin and P

parts.latex: Show that $k=4$.
Find the area enclosed between $y=kx$ and $y=12x-x^2$.

solutions.latex:
P$(8,32)$ lies on $y=kx$, so substitute it.
$$\begin{aligned} 32&=k\times 8 \\ k&=4 \end{aligned}$$

The parabola is above the line between $x=0$ and $x=8$, so the area is the integral of the difference.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^8(12x-x^2-4x)\,dx \\ &=\int_0^8(8x-x^2)\,dx \\ &=\left[4x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^8 \\ &=4(8)^2-\dfrac{8^3}{3} \\ &=256-\dfrac{512}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{256}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\dfrac{256}{3}\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct integral set up, or equivalent merit

1772_q24_1.notes: Drew y=12x-x^2 and y=4x from their equations at the crop's equal scale (14.4 px/unit), over the same window and with the same tick labels. Both graphs 0.9pt. P is a dot at the true intersection (8,32) with the label P beside it (rule 16), clear of both curves. The 0 label is moved left so it does not touch the line below the origin.
